title: What Creole means, and getting along with whites in New Orleans
summary: Asked about Creoles, Mike says the term was fluid, describes playing dances for light-skinned Creoles, then contrasts New Orleans with Mississippi and recalls a lynching story.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up under segregation: schools, neighborhoods, Jim Crow

blocks.x: Can I ask you a question that I already know the answer to and John knows the answer to, and you know the answer to, and maybe the rest of the people who might read the book,

You see, I learned—so many things change when I grow up, so I can't answer that. You know what I'm saying why I can't answer that? It's because when I was small, I thought they had white Creoles, and I thought they had light colored Creoles, and I thought they had black Creoles. So, so you know I mixed up right there, let's face it. How the hell I'm going to ask for that? How the hell I'm going to ask for that? No, no, no, wait a minute. Now wait a minute, now here's what I mean. Really? Creole? Native? Now, now, I was in some part of the society, some time that I was, but I never could stand this man, honest to God. Because my dad, man, like I said, he was a freshman. My dad taught us that a person was a person. And my dad, that's why I love him, because he did not mistreat anybody. You know what I'm saying to me? He did not put the other guy down the black, but he did not do it. That's why I love my dad, and I noticed that. I noticed that damn good. Don't you think I didn't pay attention to that when I was a kid? And that's the reason why I say so, yeah, the white Creole, and the black Creole, and the brown Creole. I dig this man. I'm like, I played at a hall, I don't recall the name, it looked like it was on Calliope Street. Some people say, some people say, Calliope. Calliope. Don't say that in New Orleans. You live in New Orleans seven years, you better not say that. Calliope. Because you say Calliope, they're cattle. They don't know what you're talking about. You know better than that. Termsicari. Do you say that in New Orleans? No. They don't even know what the hell you're talking about. Now why the hell is there that? Did you ever hear that, Calliope? Yeah. Felicity? Well, it's really Felicity, isn't it? Yeah. Technically speaking, it's Felicity. But I mean, no, but like about you say about the Creoles, man, I went, I played dances. They did. I played dances that if you walked in that place, you would know it was the white people we were praying for white people. I mean, unless somebody's told you, I bet you'd have bet your life on it. Like you say, well, who are these people? You might say, what do you mean by who are these people? I mean, we're national, there was race, something like that. Now I played dance. You know the reason why they were like that? Because they didn't lie to anybody else, is there? Let me ask you this. You understand what I mean? Mike. And they were friends for white people. Let me ask you this. What about the Irishmen? Were they still low men on the totem pole when they were youngster? Well, I can't say who was the, we had losses down there, and I can't tell them who the hell was the loss down there, of the nationality, but I know they were white, that's all I know. At least they were supposed to be white, let's put it that way. That's why they're supposed to be put in a stake about what I know. Well, the Irishmen, you know, when the potato famine happened in Ireland, a lot of them were imported into the... But I don't know, when I stopped to think, I wonder who the hell was imported to all, when they get rid of some of the bad characters, you know what I mean? Because, you know, you're taking some of the genocide, you know, I don't know how you look like, you know, well let me go, you know, you were 53, you know, you were 53, you know, you were 53, you know, you were 53, you know, you were 53. But I don't know who the hell was doing this, I don't know who was who, if there was the Irish. But, you know, there was a time when the potato famine in Ireland... But outside for that, what I mean to say, nine out of ten, if you was a guy that tended to your business with all the good color you were, nine out of ten, they didn't move all the day, they didn't all the way you, or do you any harm or anything. I remember one time, I was walking the street, one time they got strict about, well I'd already, you know, just, they come up with that stuff and they were, but they were just coming around in the Negro and they were all done. And I remember, and, and, uh, you know, when you go, I don't know how old I was, you know, when you were working, I said, I don't know how much I was. And, and, uh, well, this man didn't want nobody to call him, well I don't blame a man if you don't want nobody to give him a nickname, he used to call him Long John, he made me a cock leg. His name was John Custer, because he was a coppler at the time. You know what he said? No. He said, let him know, he said, why I let him know, what for? He said, I enjoy your little son, I know I have. He never been in trouble in his life, he just let him know. So whenever anything never come up, especially through him, I mean, like that, there's definitely another thing about you, you know, those people out there, they help you, you had a lot of them that would help you, you had a lot of them that would put their foot in your ass if they could do it. Yeah. You know, could do it. The biggest problems? But still, you still have to depend on them, you understand what I mean, Paul? The biggest problems they had on the wallets. So what I mean, but the reason why I'm bringing this up, you might say it's like a novelty or electric. It wasn't compared to the small towns. You could do that in small towns. In Mississippi?
